#5991. How Many Items Does The TSA Confiscate At US Airports Every Year?

Despite screening more than 900 million fliers annually, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) neither counts nor publishes the total number of items left behind or intercepted at US checkpoints. Every day across American airports, rushed passengers leave thousands of pocket knives, tools, and liquids in grey security bins rather than miss a flight or pay checked-bag fees. Today, the only nationwide tally tracks firearms, which increased 152% over the past decade, rising from 2,653 to 6,678 a year.

While TSA officers do not seize everyday toiletries or small tools by legal force, travelers voluntarily abandon them instead, but firearms and illegal weapons can trigger law enforcement intervention and confiscation. Before the TSA stopped logging routine surrenders in 2008, archived Bureau of Transportation Statistics records show checkpoint interceptions once topped 15 million items a year.

Since the TSA does not track everyday items, there is no federal record of how much property piles up in airport storage rooms and state warehouses each year. Meanwhile, tons of surrendered blades, tools, and liquids are weighed in bulk and hauled off with little public accounting. Tracing what happens after the checkpoint shows how local police handle intercepted guns, how new CT scanners flag prohibited items, and where surrendered knives and tools end up at state surplus auctions.

Just as commercial air travel set a new national record, federal public reporting abruptly stopped. Acting TSA chief Ha Nguyen McNeill testified in January that officers screened 906.7 million passengers and 2.1 billion carry-on bags during 2025. Yet through late 2026, the agency's newsroom still had not published a complete full-year 2025 firearm total, leaving congressional claims pointing only to a partial early tally of 2,654 incidents.

TSA estimates show rushed travelers leave 90,000 to 100,000 personal belongings behind inside screening trays each month, topping 1 million forgotten phones, laptops, keys, and belts every year. Checkpoint teams hand those items over to local airport lost-and-found offices to track down owners, while unclaimed driver's licenses and passports are shredded after 30 days. Southern US and Sunbelt hubs are responsible for an outsized share of daily gun discoveries. To the contrary, Northeastern US airports record only a tiny fraction of that rate despite serving millions more.

When an X-ray operator detects a pistol silhouette in a carry-on bag, checkpoint lanes instantaneously freeze, causing screeners to stop the belt and call armed airport police. The travelers in question allegedly claim they just forgot to properly pack the weapon in most cases. Due to these supposed oversights, the number of firearms caught annually increased from 4,432 in 2019 to a record 6,737 in 2023. In 2024, there were 6,678 detections, of which 94% arrived loaded.

Determining the probability of a gun surfacing in the checkpoint of a US Airport can be predicted largely based on the geographical location of the airfield. Regional airport police data has been used to confirm that loaded handguns continue to pour into terminals around the country despite Washington's missing annual summary. Even with that national data gap, firearm interceptions indicate a trend based more on individual locations rather than passenger volume.

With 440 intercepted firearms in 2024, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) led the US, surpassing Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW) at 390. Meanwhile, Houston Intercontinental (IAH) reported 272 and Phoenix Sky Harbor (PHX) claimed 247 firearm interceptions. In January 2025, Atlanta TSA Federal Security Director Robert Spinden clarified that eight New England airports combined stopped fewer than 50 firearms out of 33 million passengers.

Yet, liquid rules still strip far more everyday items from carry-on bags than firearm catches ever will. This has become a point of confusion for international travelers as European hubs in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, and Dublin rolled out new scanners allowing fliers to carry bottles up to 67.6 ounces (2 liters). American checkpoints still force travelers to dump water and toiletries because domestic scanners lack the cleared software and funding needed to inspect large containers.

Water bottles outrank every weapon TSA finds. Here are the five items most often surrendered at US checkpoints.

In the early years following September 11, airports recorded nearly every prohibited item removed from carry-on bags. In 2003, they intercepted 6.1 million items. In 2005, when the TSA banned cigarette lighters, they reached an all-time high of 15,887,596. Millions of individual shampoo bottles, pocket knives, and wrenches were logged, quickly overcrowding checkpoint lanes.

Even in the wake of a 2006 bombing attempt, which inspired the 3-1-1 rule capping liquid bottles at 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters), lifting the lighter ban in 2007 reduced total seizures to 6.5 million a year. Then, on August 8, 2008, the TSA quietly stopped collecting national counts for almost every category, tracking only firearms and incendiaries before cutting public reports to just guns after 2010.

Overnight, federal bookkeeping vanished across hundreds of terminals, leaving lawmakers and travelers blind to the true scale of property being seized. Instead of counting individual tools or blades, checkpoints began weighing surrendered gear in bulk before hauling it off to state surplus. That reporting blackout obscures a massive waste and resale pipeline running behind across the country. Meanwhile, TSA officers simultaneously confronted a decade-long surge in firearms discovered in carry-on luggage across the US.

A closer look at the top ten airports where TSA discovers loaded firearms reveals stark differences in gun safety across the US.

Although the criminal penalties differ greatly per airport, when officers find a firearm, the checkpoint stops, and local police take over. For instance, only two of the 87 handgun detections at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in the first four months of 2025 were prosecuted by Atlanta police. Most of the time, travelers were permitted to leave the airport and secure their firearms inside parked cars. Regardless of local charges, the TSA imposes a more stringent penalty, suspending TSA PreCheck access for a minimum of five years and collecting civil fines totaling more than $52 million over a three-year period.

Everyday prohibited items, like pocket knives, heavy wrenches, and multitools—follow a much quieter path after being dropped into checkpoint bins. Rather than going into evidence lockers, surrendered gear sits in airport storage before being transferred to state surplus agencies for public auction.

New England TSA spokesperson Dan Velez described the handoff to Reader's Digest: "We collect that stuff for anywhere from one to three months, and then a state surplus store will come by. We give all the stuff that was surrendered to the state surplus store, and they auction it off." State surplus offices bundle those blades and tools by the pound on government auction sites like GovDeals and keep the proceeds, with Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) alone turning over roughly 4,000 pounds (1.8 metric tons) of surrendered items each year.

Meanwhile, the checkpoint bottlenecks driving many of those surrenders persist largely because federal screening upgrades remain underfunded. Every airline passenger pays a $5.60 September 11 security fee per one-way trip, yet Congress routinely diverts roughly a third of that revenue, about $1.6 billion annually, toward federal deficit reduction rather than spending it on new 3D scanners and checkpoint staffing.

The 100ml rule is finally being scrapped after last year's false start.

Newer 3D computed tomography (CT) scanners were supposed to end the misery of unpacking laptops and toiletries at airport checkpoints, yet travelers often find their bags pulled aside for secondary searches more frequently than before. Unlike older 2D X-ray tunnels that only show flat shadows from two fixed angles, CT machines spin an X-ray gantry around the bag to build a full 3D model, allowing officers to rotate images on screen and spot pocket knives, tools, or liquids hidden behind dense batteries.

Although fewer forbidden objects pass through undetected thanks to this clearer perspective, it also sets off a lot more automated alerts on commonplace, innocuous objects. Commonplace objects like thick hardcover books, blocks of cheese, dense protein bars, or tangled charging cords are frequently marked for manual examination because CT software assesses object density in addition to shape. Officers manually unpack bags that are diverted to the secondary search table, frequently finding loose ammunition, oversized toiletries, or forgotten multitools hidden at the bottom of a rucksack that a flat 2D X-ray could have overlooked.

Confusion over screening standards contributes to the pileup. Even at the 296 airports where the TSA has deployed 1,162 CT units, the agency maintains a 3.4-ounce (100-milliliter) limit on carry-on liquids because most US checkpoints still employ antiquated X-ray lanes. Travelers who believe the new scanners allow full-sized water bottles or pricey fragrances through security frequently realize, at the end of the belt, that the liquids must still be dumped or scrutinized.

Meanwhile, the entire checkpoint is slowed down by the hardware's physical footprint. In order to obtain high-resolution scans, CT scanners from manufacturers such as Smiths Detection, Analogic, and L3Harris employ slower conveyor belts and weigh between 4,299 and 5,401 pounds (1,950 and 2,450 kg) each. As a result of fewer bags being moved per minute and more bags being diverted for hand searches, lines quickly reform, forcing hurried travelers to immediately abandon flagged items rather than risk missing their flight by getting out of line to check a bag.

#5988. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#5987. Air Canada Launches 12 New International Routes: See Full List Now

Air Canada is set to expand its international network considerably in 2027, with 12 new routes scheduled that were absent from its network in 2026. Aeroroutes reports that the additions will include nine routes that are entirely new to the airline and three returning services, including one that Canada's flag carrier last operated a quarter of a century ago.

Europe accounts for half of the additions, while Air Canada is also expanding its presence in the US, Mexico, China, and Israel. The growth is being facilitated by new aircraft deliveries, most notably the Airbus A321XLR. However, the airline's expanding international network is also benefiting from additional widebody capacity.

Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) is the biggest beneficiary of the expansion by route count, with six of the 12 additions. Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) follows with four, while Vancouver and Edmonton each gain one. All but one of the routes will launch before the end of June, with Montréal–Seville following in September.

Of the three returning routes, Toronto–Louisville has had the longest absence, having last operated in June 2002. Toronto–Shannon returns after it only had a single summer season in 2018, when it was operated by the Boeing 737 MAX 8. Meanwhile, Montréal–Tel Aviv was inaugurated in June 2017 before being suspended in October 2023 following the outbreak of conflict in Israel.

Among the entirely new routes, Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport (CAN) will become Air Canada's third mainland Chinese destination, complementing Beijing and Shanghai. Basel will similarly become its third Swiss destination, while Seville will gain its first nonstop transatlantic service. Mark Galardo, Air Canada's Chief Commercial Officer, said the additions reflect the airline's ambitions to reach underserved markets:

"Summer 2027 marks the most extensive intercontinental expansion in Air Canada’s history. Enabled by the next-generation capabilities of our expanding Airbus A321XLR fleet, the likes of Seville builds upon recent additions to Palma de Mallorca and Tenerife."

Four of the 12 additions, including two-thirds of the new European routes, will be operated by the Airbus A321XLR. Air Canada took delivery of its first of 30 examples in April this year, with the aircraft making its transatlantic debut between Montréal and Toulouse in June. It has since enabled further expansion into secondary European markets.

Configured with 182 seats, including 14 lie-flat business class seats, the aircraft allows Air Canada to serve markets where demand might not justify a widebody. Speaking at last week's Scotiabank Transportation & Industrials Conference, CFO John Di Bert revealed that the airline's 2026 route launches were performing in the upper half of its margin range:

"They have been accretive new routes, and we are confident that the next batch of routes will also be accretive."

XLR Routes Introduced Or Scheduled In 2026

Berlin, Lisbon, Lyon, Nantes, Porto, Tenerife, Toulouse

Amsterdam, Basel, Dublin, Edinburgh, Seville

Air Canada currently plans to deploy the A321XLR on 20 transatlantic routes in 2027. Its role extends beyond opening new markets, with Air Canada also replacing some Boeing 787 services with A321XLRs. This releases widebody capacity for longer or higher-demand routes, particularly across the Pacific, where the Dreamliner is central to the airline's expansion.

The airline is optimizing its network and growing all-around, with both types becoming integral to its plans.

Air Canada's growth extends well beyond the 12 new routes. Next summer, it plans to operate more than 125 international routes outside of routes to the US, offering up to 169,000 weekly seats across more than 85 destinations. This represents an increase of over 8% in available seat miles (ASMs), driven partly by increased frequencies and extended seasonal services.

Alongside additional A321XLR deliveries, the imminent arrival of Air Canada's Boeing 787-10s will provide further opportunities for international expansion. The airline has 14 examples on order, with two scheduled for delivery before the end of this year and six more in 2027. Management expects approximately two-thirds of next year's incremental capacity to be allocated to international markets.

Under its New Frontiers growth strategy, Air Canada is targeting more than 130 billion ASMs by 2030, up from approximately 108 billion this year. Having already substantially expanded its international network in 2026, the carrier has indicated that further network announcements will accompany its incoming aircraft deliveries. As such, the 12 additions reported here are likely just the starting point for an even fuller 2027 expansion.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Cool that AC is adding transatlantic/pacific routes to destinations that didn't have one

#5986. Your complete guide to the ALL Accor hotel loyalty program

Answer a few questions and get your top card matches for earning maximum rewards.

Compare the cost of booking with points to cash.

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

Katie Genter is a digital nomad who has traveled full time since June 2017. She writes and edits stories about points and miles, and loyalty programs, often letting her personal experiences color these stories.

By commenting, you agree to our Community Guidelines to help create a positive space for conversation. They have not been reviewed, approved, or otherwise endorsed by any of these parties. All responses are submitted by individual contributors, and neither the bank advertiser, our partners, nor TPG are responsible for ensuring that all posts and/or questions are answered.... Read more

ALL Accor reward points have a fixed value when you redeem them toward eligible hotel stays: 1,000 points get you 20 euros off. That gives each reward point a hotel stay value of 2 euro cents and is why TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Accor points at 2.25 cents.

ALL Accor reward points expire after 365 consecutive days without eligible point-earning activity. Any qualifying activity that credits at least one reward point extends the validity of your entire balance for another 365 days. An eligible donation of reward points can also extend the validity of your balance.

ALL Accor doesn't price hotel awards as traditional free nights. Instead, you can generally redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay. When redeeming online, you can use 1,000 points for 20 euros off or 2,000 points for 40 euros off; after that, redemption amounts generally increase in increments of 2,000 points.

You can earn ALL Accor Silver, Gold or Platinum status through either status nights or status points within a calendar year. Silver requires 10 nights or 2,000 status points, Gold requires 30 nights or 7,000 status points, and Platinum requires 60 nights or 14,000 status points. Diamond status requires 26,000 status points and can't be earned through nights alone, while Limitless status is available by invitation only.

An eligible stay paid for in part or in full with reward points can still earn status nights. However, you'll only earn reward points and status points on the eligible portion of the bill that you pay without reward points.

Accor may not have the same name recognition or footprint in the U.S. as some other major hotel groups, but its portfolio may be difficult to ignore if you travel internationally. Its brands range from luxury names such as Raffles and Fairmont to budget-friendly options such as Ibis.

The ALL Accor loyalty program works differently from many hotel programs familiar to U.S. travelers. Reward points have a fixed value in euros toward most eligible hotel stays, elite status can be earned through nights or eligible spending, and paid memberships can help you save on stays and accelerate your progress toward status.

Here's what you need to know about earning and redeeming ALL Accor points, qualifying for elite status and deciding whether the program is a good fit for you.

ALL Accor is the hotel loyalty program for Accor Group. The program covers over 5,800 hotels across more than 45 brands in 110-plus countries worldwide, ranging from Fairmont and Pullman to Mercure and Ibis.

Accor has an especially strong footprint in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Asia-Pacific region. Its comparatively limited North American footprint makes ALL Accor less appealing to many U.S.-based travelers.

You can become a member of ALL Accor by visiting the program's website and clicking the sign-up button in the upper-right corner. From there, it's a quick and easy process to sign up for the free-to-join ALL Accor program.

You'll see two different points balances in your ALL Accor account: reward points and status points. Reward points are what you can redeem for stays and other rewards, while status points are one of the ways you can earn ALL Accor status.

When you book an eligible stay — which generally excludes stays booked through online travel agencies — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, as well as status points based on the brand and your eligible pretax spending.

Specifically, here's how many reward points and status points you'll earn per 10 euros (about $11) spent:

So, a Classic member staying at an Adagio Access property would earn 500 reward points and 500 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending, while a Diamond elite member would earn double the reward points but the same number of status points. Meanwhile, 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending at a Fairmont would earn 2,500 status points regardless of elite tier, but a Classic member would earn 2,500 reward points while a Diamond elite member would earn 5,000 reward points.

Accor has more than 45 brands; here's an overview of the Accor Group brands:

However, not all of these brands participate fully in ALL Accor. The list of excluded hotels and brands is rather long, but note that no HotelF1 properties participate, most Ibis Budget properties are excluded and only select The Hoxton hotels participate.

ALL Accor also includes select third-party “Partner of ALL Accor” properties. Earning and elite benefits may vary at these hotels, and reward points can't be used to reduce the cost of stays at IntercityHotel, Steigenberger, Steigenberger Icon, Maxx, Jaz in the City or Zleep properties.

The ALL Accor hotel loyalty program has an entry tier, four earnable elite status tiers and an invitation-only Limitless tier. Members can also benefit from select paid memberships and occasional status match or challenge opportunities.

Status nights and status points reset at the start of each calendar year. Once you reach a new tier, you'll keep it for the rest of that calendar year and the following calendar year. To retain it beyond then, you must requalify during the next calendar year.

ALL Accor members have Classic status if they don't qualify for elite status. So, as soon as you join ALL Accor, you'll enjoy Classic benefits, including:

You can earn ALL Accor Silver status when you stay 10 nights or earn 2,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Classic members, Silver elite members get the following perks:

If you happen to have Gold status with Qatar Airways Privilege Club, you can link your account with ALL Accor and upgrade to Silver status after your first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Gold status when you stay 30 nights or earn 7,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Silver elite members, Gold elite members get the following perks:

Some cards issued outside the U.S. offer ALL Accor Gold status as a cardmember perk, though none issued in the U.S. currently do. And Qatar Airways Privilege Club Platinum members can upgrade to ALL Accor Gold status after their first eligible international hotel stay with Accor.

You can earn ALL Accor Platinum status when you stay 60 nights or earn 14,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Gold elite members, Platinum elite members get the following perks:

Once you reach 60 nights or 14,000 status points within a calendar year, you'll earn two suite night upgrades. Each suite night upgrade guarantees a one-night upgrade to a suite. You can earn an additional suite night upgrade for every additional 4,000 status points you earn.

You can earn ALL Accor Diamond status when you accrue at least 26,000 status points within a calendar year. In addition to benefits available to Platinum elite members, Diamond elite members get the following perks:

ALL Accor also has an invitation-only Limitless status, which Accor grants at its discretion. In addition to all the Diamond benefits, Limitless members get 24-hour access to a personal assistant and concierge service, can gift Platinum status to a person of their choice and can transfer reward points to as many as five other ALL Accor members (up to 12 transfers per year).

ALL Accor offers three paid ALL Accor+ memberships: ALL Accor+ Explorer, ALL Accor+ Voyager and ALL Accor+ Ibis.

These subscriptions offer discounts, a boost toward higher elite status and various other perks. Although ALL Accor+ subscriptions can be combined, ALL Accor caps the bonus status nights you can receive from subscription programs and cobranded cards at 30 per account, per calendar year.

I've considered buying the ALL Accor+ Ibis membership, as its 15% discount could cover the 99-euro annual fee once you spend about 660 euros on eligible stays booked at the subscription rate.

You have many opportunities to earn reward points and status points with Accor. Here's an overview of the options most relevant for U.S. residents.

When you book an eligible stay — which excludes stays booked through online travel websites — you'll earn reward points based on the brand, your status tier and your eligible pretax spending, plus status points based on the brand and the cost of your stay. Specifically, Classic members earn reward points and status points as follows:

Elite members earn additional reward points on top of what Classic members earn; Silver members get 24% additional reward points, Gold members get 48% additional reward points, Platinum members get 76% additional reward points, and Diamond and Limitless members get 100% additional reward points. However, elite members don't earn any additional status points over what Classic members earn.

So, while a Classic member would earn 1,250 reward points and 1,250 status points on 1,000 euros of eligible pretax spending on an Ibis stay, a Platinum member would earn 2,200 reward points and 1,250 status points on the same stay.

You'll earn reward points and status points not just for your room but also for meals, minibar, spa and other eligible charges to your room. Plus, if you opt to Skip the Clean, you'll earn 100 reward points per day skipped. And keep in mind that you can earn reward points — but not status points or nights — on day rooms at participating Accor properties.

You can earn reward points on rental cars from three partners as follows:

You can earn reward points by clicking through the Collections site before shopping.

You can earn up to 600 reward points on your first survey with Club Opinions. And with e-Rewards, you can earn 250 reward points on your first survey.

You can convert the following transferable rewards into ALL Accor reward points as follows:

Transfers are final, though, so make sure converting your rewards to ALL Accor is the best-value option before you transfer.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

You can earn reward points as follows when you convert select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards:

After linking your ALL Accor account with an eligible airline loyalty account, you may be able to earn reward points on select flights in addition to the rewards you earn with the airline program. For example, you can earn 1 reward point per $2 spent on eligible Qatar Airways flights and 1 reward point per 2 euros spent on eligible Air France-KLM flights.

Elite members with Gold status or higher in ALL Accor or Qantas Frequent Flyer can earn 1 reward point per 4 Australian dollars (about $3) spent on eligible Qantas flights, while ALL Accor members with Silver status or higher and Azul Fidelidade members with Diamante status can earn 1 reward point for every 7.50 euros spent on eligible Azul flights.

You can earn 1 reward point and 1 status point per 2 euros spent when you host a group of at least eight attendees (or at least eight rooms) at a participating hotel. It doesn't matter whether your event is a professional gathering or personal celebration.

You have plenty of options for redeeming Accor points. As with earning, we'll focus on redemptions most relevant to U.S. residents.

ALL Accor lets you redeem 1,000 reward points for 20 euros off an eligible stay at a participating hotel. You can use points toward part or, in some cases, all of your stay, although some prepaid rates require a portion to be paid by card.

To redeem points for a hotel stay online, log in to your ALL Accor account and search for a stay as normal. When you choose a rate at a specific hotel, look for one with a purple "Pay with your points" designation if you want to redeem points for part or all of your stay.

Near the end of the booking process, you can opt to redeem points toward your stay. For example, I could redeem 1,000 points for 20 euros off my stay and pay the remaining balance with a credit card.

These hotel stay redemptions provide a fixed value of 2 euro cents per point, so you generally won't get outsize value from your reward points.

You can redeem — and, in some cases, bid — Accor points for select entertainment, dining and sports experiences through the ALL Limitless Experiences page. There are some great deals to be found, too, such as this Christmas Eve dinner for just 600 points.

You can also redeem Accor points for select activities through ALL Accor Activities & Events.

It's worth checking both of these programs periodically to see whether any experiences fit your upcoming schedule and tastes.

You can redeem your Accor reward points for select types of airline and train loyalty program rewards as follows:

I don't usually recommend transferring hotel points to other travel loyalty programs, as you'll typically lose a good bit of value. Check TPG's valuations and calculate your redemption rate before transferring ALL Accor points to another program.

ALL Accor is most compelling for travelers who frequently visit Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region, where Accor has a much larger footprint than in North America. Its hotel redemptions are also easy to understand: 1,000 reward points generally get you 20 euros off an eligible stay.

However, that simplicity means you generally won't find the outsize hotel redemptions that are possible with programs that use award charts or dynamic pricing. ALL Accor also lacks a U.S.-issued cobranded credit card, and its U.S.-accessible transfer partners generally transfer at less than a 1:1 ratio.

Elite status can still be useful, especially at the Platinum and Diamond levels, which offer perks such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast in certain regions or on certain days. Finally, ALL Accor+ subscriptions may be useful for some travelers.

ALL Accor probably won't be the best primary hotel program for most U.S.-based travelers given its relatively limited North American footprint, lack of a U.S.-issued cobranded card and less-than-1:1 transfer ratios. But it may be useful if you frequently stay at Accor brands in Europe, the Middle East, Africa or the Asia-Pacific region.

Reward points are easy to use at a fixed value toward eligible hotel stays, while higher elite tiers offer potentially valuable benefits such as lounge access, suite night upgrades and complimentary breakfast. Frequent Accor guests should consider whether an ALL Accor+ subscription could pay for itself through discounts, status nights and other benefits.

Even if you don't plan to pursue status, it's worth joining ALL Accor before your next eligible stay to access member rates and earn reward points.

#5985. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#5984. Storms Cancel Flights As 80 Million Americans Travel For Thanksgiving

FlightAware data shows hundreds of canceled and delayed flights in the US today due to poor weather conditions. There have been 396 cancellations already for flights within, into, or out of the United States. More have been delayed, with 1,053 flights within, into, or out of the US facing this type of disruption.

The troublesome weather is the result of two areas of low pressure arriving at American shores, one off the northwest coast and one off the northeast coast. It comes at the worst possible time, with over 80 million Americans expected to travel across the Thanksgiving weekend.

The FAA has said it is the busiest holiday travel weekend in 16 years, yet it will be heavily disrupted by the weather. On the East Coast, streets are submerged in the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area. To the west in Huntington Beach, California, floodwaters have also covered roads and entered homes. Coastal areas have been hit particularly hard, with huge waves striking much of the coastline. New York City and New Jersey have declared states of emergency, with an official stating at a press conference, "This is a serious storm that requires us all to exercise caution."The table below shows the origin airports that have seen the most canceled and delayed flights today, making use of FlightAware data:

Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA)

Anybody who has experienced the ongoing poor weather will be unsurprised that aircraft have not been able to begin their scheduled services. "[It is] absolutely craziness, but the end goal is what it is all about, just to get home," one traveler told TODAY.

The FAA had previously warned that forecast rain and winds made delays possible "throughout the week" due to the poor weather. On Wednesday, FlightAware data showed over 6,800 delays and over 60 cancellations.

The most eye-catching and worrying event from Wednesday was the overshoot of a runway at Miami International Airport (MIA) by a McDonnell Douglas MD-11, operated by FedEx Express. The incident involving a 34-year-old aircraft led the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to impose a ground stop, disrupting many Thanksgiving travelers hoping to beat the weekend rush.

MIA reopened on Wednesday night, but was still short of full capacity with two runways available. Delays overnight exceeded three hours. By early morning today, the average delay was three hours and 34 minutes.

New York has one of the most complex and congested airspaces in the country.

The US government had taken steps to minimize disruptions during the Thanksgiving weekend following the four-hour nationwide ground stop on November 13. Top officials from the FAA, the Department of Defense, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the Department of Transportation (DOT) were put together in a "Tiger Team" that met weekly in the run-up to Thanksgiving. With the DOT refusing to rule out further ground stops while systems are updated, their role was to ensure that any disruption came outside of Thanksgiving.

White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told the Daily Wire:

“President Trump and [Transportation] Secretary [Sean] Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened last Friday can never happen again."

Preventing nationwide ground stops caused by human or technological issues is possible. However, the impact of severe weather is harder to mitigate. While any cancellations and ground stops caused by this week's storms will be localized rather than causing a nationwide halt to aviation, there is next to nothing that the top team set up for this week can do about it.

#5983. Island Mayor Pleads With Japan Airlines Mileage Runners After Locals Can’t Book Flights

The concept of mileage running is making headlines in Japan, and not in a good way. A lucrative promotion from Japan Airlines reportedly caused passengers to take up to 12 flights per day in remote markets, in some cases making it difficult for locals to book flights. What a story this is!

News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused issues for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

This ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

At Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:

The issue is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:

Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”

Japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

I think this story is a good reminder of just how well frequent flyer programs can work with the purpose of filling seats on planes… for better or worse!

While it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a new restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the issue here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

What do you make of this Japan Airlines mileage run promotion situation?

#5981. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:

“The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the company has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”

Tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG

Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

I am curious if there were some new policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

Israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

I added the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card to my wallet over 10 years ago for its simple earning rates and modest $95 annual fee.

It has remained a valuable mid-tier travel rewards card due to its straightforward earning rates and no foreign transaction fees. Plus, you have multiple ways to redeem your rewards, including covering recent travel purchases at a fixed rate and transferring your miles to any of the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel partners.

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it an excellent everyday spending card. Plus, it offers 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel. These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards card an appealing and good option for consumers who want to use one card for all their purchases.

Unlike many of the other best everyday spending cards, the Venture Rewards card stands out by offering no foreign transaction fees. The card carries a $95 annual fee but offers a $50 experience credit on every Lifestyle Collection booking, complimentary Hertz Five Star status and up to a $120 statement credit (every four years) when you use your Venture card to apply for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck. Plus, cardholders enjoy price prediction and free price drop protection when booking flights through Capital One Travel.

The Capital One Venture Rewards earns miles that you can redeem for travel, cash back, gift cards, experiences and more. But you can also transfer your miles to 15-plus travel loyalty programs, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Choice Privileges.

Related: 7 reasons to get the Capital One Venture Rewards card

Related: Why I keep the Capital One Venture Rewards card in my wallet

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers cardholders several benefits that help offset the card's $95 annual fee.

One of my favorite benefits of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the price prediction and free price drop protection that's available when I book flights through Capital One Travel.

The price prediction appears anytime you search for a flight through Capital One Travel. It provides guidance on whether to book now and also estimates how pricing is likely to change if you wait to book.

If the price prediction advises booking now, Capital One Travel will automatically apply price drop protection to that purchase at no additional charge. Then, you'll receive up to $50 of the difference back if the price drops within 10 days.

These two features often give me the confidence I need to book or continue to track prices. I've gotten money back on several flights via the automated price drop protection, which is always a nice surprise.

You also have some protection if you book a flight, hotel or rental car through Capital One Travel and then find a better price for the same flight, hotel or rental car on another site within 24 hours of booking. Specifically, you can call Capital One Travel, submit a price match claim and then get a travel credit for the difference if the agent can verify the lower price.

I've successfully done price match guarantees for several flights, with the phone calls often taking under 10 minutes. Keep in mind, though, that the itinerary must be an exact match to what you booked on Capital One Travel, and you must submit your claim within 24 hours of making your reservation through Capital One Travel. The price must be in dollars and available to the general public without any coupons, promotions or member discounts.

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders receive up to a $120 statement credit for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck (every four years). The credit will apply to whichever program is applied to first, so consider your application timing if you plan to pay for applications to both programs with your card.

I love having Global Entry, as it lets me get through U.S. immigration queues quickly, and it also gives me TSA PreCheck. I'd pay the Global Entry application fee even if my Capital One Venture Rewards card didn't offer a statement credit, so this perk effectively gives me up to $120 back (every four years).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status through the "Benefits" tab of the Capital One website or mobile app. However, it may take up to 72 hours after you register for Hertz status for the upgrade to take effect, so don't wait until you're about to pick up your rental car to register.

I like having Hertz Five Star status, as it provides upgrades when available, 25% more points and a wider choice of vehicles at Ultimate Choice locations.

Each time you make an eligible Lifestyle Collection booking through Capital One Travel, you'll get a $50 experience credit to enjoy during your stay. The booking must be made in the cardholder's name, and the cardholder must be staying on the eligible booking.

If you are staying at a hotel, the hotel will apply the credit at checkout to qualifying charges up to $50. Ask the hotel which purchases qualify, then charge them to your room.

If you're staying at a vacation rental, the host will apply the credit when you book an eligible experience with a Capital One credit card. However, at some vacation rental properties, you may get the experience credit as a gift card.

You'll also enjoy other perks on eligible Lifestyle Collection stays, including complimentary Wi-Fi, early check-in and late checkout. However, early check-in and late checkout are only provided when available, and bookings may have a minimum stay requirement. At hotels, you are also eligible for a room upgrade (subject to availability).

Capital One Venture Rewards cardholders also get access to Capital One Dining and Capital One Entertainment.

The entertainment platform may be your ticket to cardholder-only VIP packages and hard-to-secure tickets to popular games, concerts and shows.

Meanwhile, the dining platform can help you secure hard-to-get reservations at top restaurants and provide access to exclusive dining events.

Related: Is the Capital One Venture Rewards card worth it?

Capital One miles are easy to earn and redeem yet still offer significant value. Here's what you should know about earning and redeeming Capital One miles.

The Capital One Venture Rewards offers simple-to-remember earning rates. Specifically, you'll earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases.

These earning rates make the Capital One Venture Rewards an excellent option, whether it's your only card or you use it primarily for purchases that wouldn't earn bonus rewards on other cards. I often use my Capital One Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar spent if I used another rewards credit card.

One of the big positives of the Capital One Venture Rewards is the flexibility of its miles. However, the two best ways to redeem Capital One miles are to cover recent travel purchases and to transfer miles to select airline or hotel loyalty programs.

Redeeming Capital One miles to cover recent travel purchases gives you 1 cent per mile and is incredibly easy. Once you make an eligible travel purchase with your card, you'll have 90 days to log into the Capital One app or website and redeem rewards to cover your purchase.

However, I prefer to redeem my miles by transferring them to the 15-plus Capital One airline and hotel program partners. Some of my favorite options include Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Air Canada Aeroplan and Avianca LifeMiles, but you also have access to JetBlue TrueBlue, Wyndham Rewards and many other programs.

I recently redeemed 80,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points (plus $85 in taxes and fees) to fly business class from Cape Town to Perth, Australia, on an itinerary that would have otherwise cost over $2,200.

As long as you get more than 1 cent per mile when transferring miles to partners, this is the most valuable redemption option. However, TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents each. So, you'll usually want to choose airline or hotel programs that offer at least this much value for your miles when you transfer them.

Related: Have the Capital One Venture Rewards Card but new to points and miles? Here’s what you need to know

The Capital One Venture Rewards won't be the right card for everyone. Here are some drawbacks to keep in mind:

If the lack of airport lounge benefits and potential difficulty in offsetting the annual fee are your primary concerns about the Capital One Venture, it may be worth considering the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card instead.

The Capital One Venture X has a higher annual fee ($395) than the Venture ($95), but it offers $300 in annual credits toward bookings made through Capital One Travel. Therefore, if you can naturally use the Venture X's full $300 annual Capital One Travel credit, it can effectively narrow the difference between the cards' annual fees to $0.

Venture X cardholders also get 10,000 bonus miles on each account anniversary, starting with the first anniversary. Between the bonus miles and the annual travel credit, most consumers will get more value than the card's annual fee each year.

Plus, the Venture X offers 10 miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel, 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel and 2 miles per dollar spent on all other purchases. Capital One Venture X cardholders also get access to Priority Pass lounges and Capital One lounges.

#5979. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.
