#5941. Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

Back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways announced it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

Earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an update on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:

The Company’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the company was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,…

So while the company hasn’t formally announced that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline launched in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline update its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

The company got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

Since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “new” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

Norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

Could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the company’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

Financial issues at the company started when… well, it launched. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

#5940. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

What do you make of this FedEx MD-11 accident in Miami?

#5939. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

#5937. American Airlines Pilots And Flight Attendants Unite To Demand New Leadership—Say They’re Done Asking Management To Do Better

Five days after American Airlines announced it was replacing Chief Operating Officer, the flight attendants and pilots unions say that change at the top needs to go further. And they’re making this case in part based on American’s poor recovery from this month’s FAA nationwide ground stop. Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want. “American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

Captain Nick Silva of the Allied Pilots Association and Julie Hedrick of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants signed a joint letter that both unions sent out. They tell management, “We have spent years asking you to do better. Those days are over.” A few lines later they say what they want.

“American Airlines needs a new direction — and leadership capable of delivering it.”

In February, the flight attendants’ union board voted unanimously that it had no confidence in Robert Isom. Pilots did not go as far.

And today’s note is being misinterpreted by some as a call for Isom to go. Today’s letter leaves his name out of it, never naming him at all. It’s actually a weaker call than they made earlier in the year.

This gives the unions room to claim a win even if Isom stays CEO. As I wrote earlier today, American may be looking for an outside president who could eventually succeed Isom, and former Wall Street Journal airline reporter Scott McCartney says a hire could come by year-end.

The unions circulated FlightAware data compiled by BofA Global Research. On Saturday, American canceled 42% of its mainline flights, Delta 28% and United 26%. By Sunday, Delta was down to 5%. However, The chart is misleading by picking only two U.S. airlines and mainline flights only. JetBlue cancelled 44% of flights over the 3 days. They left JetBlue off the chart. Including regional flights, American, United and Delta all performed similarly – American cancelled 28.5%, Delta 25.1%, and United 23%. So the union heads are cherry picking by focusing only on mainline. (American even owns three of its regional carriers.) After Winter Storm Fern at the start of the year, I obtained minutes from a flight attendants’ union executive committee meeting. Hedrick said American sent crews to a service center that couldn’t actually book hotel rooms. What struck me at the time was how much sympathy she had for management. On November 15, her union reported that flight attendants waited hours to get their trip assignments fixed, then waited again for rooms. Some never got one. American needed those same people rested to fly passengers the next day. The unions take a swipe in their note at American investing in better seats and lounges. They need those to generate more revenue. Silva himself said in September he wished American had started investing in customers years earlier. What Each Union Gets Out Of Signing Hedrick’s union is helping members claim compensation for hotel delays and get their expenses reimbursed. Having pilots back them publicly helps her bargaining position. She comes out looking tough, even though the note doesn’t go nearly as far as the union went in calling for leadership change earlier in the year. Silva gets a second union making his case that the people who fly the schedule know where it breaks. He opened contract talks a year early and asked for a seat on American’s board. When the pilots asked to make their case to the directors in February, the board sent them back to management. Weak profits are hurting employees. American paid 0.3% of eligible 2025 earnings in profit sharing. On $50,000 that’s $150. At Delta the same earnings would’ve meant $4,450. American already pays competitive pilot wages. I’d expect this negotiation to focus on quality of life issues rather than big raises. But the union is positioning itself to argue that management is at fault for poor performance, shouldn’t get to use that as an excuse for being unable to afford contract concessions, and the union is in fact part of the answer. United pilots got board representation in a 1994 employee buyout involving wage and work rule concessions. They kept it through bankruptcy as part of $1.1 billion in concessions. Delta pilots gained a voting seat in the Northwest merger deal. American’s pilots don’t have a transaction like that to bargain over. Meanwhile, the fight inside their independent union over joining the larger Air Line Pilots Association helped cost Silva’s predecessor his job. Silva wants to show effectiveness taking on management to keep his job.. Another pretty scathing letter put out by the Flight Attendants and Pilots Union at AA calling for new leadership — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 25, 2026 I wrote back in February that the unions would want credit for any change they saw coming. If American names a president in the coming weeks, Silva and Hedrick get to claim a victory and they’ve laid down a marker for what that leader needs to focus on. Against my better judgement (and because I had limited choice) I flew AA last week up front. It was uninspired service as usual. Pretty rich from the unions that put themselves over the paying passengers or won’t do pre departure beverage or won’t help clients at a gate

Scott Kirbys CEO job need to go and we need to get a honest person to run united. Employee’s and people are tired of dishonest crooks run a company for there own gains. Scott Kirby supports a big CROOK so what does that say about Kirby. He needs to go ASAP

Due to the fact that AA is the dominant airlines at KMIA – I fly with them quite often. Every time I travel with AA I speak with the employees, from the ticket counter, gate, Flight Attendants and Pilots and, so far, NOT ONE has had anything good to say about Isom and the useless management tam or the board of directors. These idiots have been driving AA into the ULLC realm for years now and it reflects in the attitude of all the employees.

GET RID OF THE BOARD, CEO AND ENTIRE TOP MANAGEMENT TEAM!!

In most real world jobs, employees who bad mouth or otherwise undermine their employees tend to get fired. Management should absolutely take responsibility for its role in American’s under performance, But much of the blame also lies with employees who simply don’t appear to be doing their jobs. I wouldn’t be surprised if a fairly large number of American’s employees aren’t deliberately sabotaging the airline to spite management. I hope I’m 1000% wrong about that last sentence, but deliberate actions that undermine employers aren’t unheard of in unionized work forces.

Maybe change at the top is needed but the AA crew I’ve experienced need to go to. Most miserable, passive aggressive old female flight attendants I have ever met on a flight this year from New Zealand to LAX. No, they don’t need motivation from the top or retraining .. just dismissing as they were all terrible ambassadors for AA (and US customer service in general). We were genuinely shocked just how awful they were.

You won’t get arguments from me as far as AA’s mgmt and board being incompetent and overpaid. But as others have said AA’s inflight, union provided, service has sucked for at least the last 25 years. The first bunch of times I flew biz and first to Japan I was shocked by the surliness and unhelpfulness of the fat granny FA’s. I can’t blame FA’s for being demoralized now, given the mgmt (not leadership), and some are pretty good, but most are lazy and disengaged. Hard to imagine this lot providing premium service regardless of who is in charge or how much they’re paid. Pls queue up 1990 to tell us how unions are held down by “the man”.

Blah blah blah management couldn’t care less. Now open up that can of soda and clean the toilet

Pretty rich coming from the ranks .. AA turned our recent travel into a nightmare of cancellations, delays, agonizingly long queues, incompetence, arrogance and expensive unplanned hotel stays. The cerry on the cake: 5 hours 51 minutes on hold to get a missed flight rebooked.

To channel James Carville: “It’s the shareholders, stupid.” Nothing will improve until the entire Board of Directors is overturned like the rotten apple cart it is. That’s where the unions should be pleading their loudest case of all.

FWIW, AA did do a little worse than DL and UA recovering from last week’s FAA ground stop. But they often do better than their competitors recovering from other irregular opps like snowstorms. I don’t think anyone could legitimately complain that THIS is a major AA weakness.

The people complaining about pre-departure beverages and inconsistent service don’t understand how poorly the airline is run behind the scenes. FAs barely have enough time to get on the plane, check their safety equipment and stow their luggage before the gate agent starts throwing passengers on. Half the time catering hasn’t even shown up yet, and when it does, something is inevitably missing or wrong. American expects excellence from its employees but doesn’t give them the time, staffing or resources to actually deliver it.

Are there shitty FAs at American? Absolutely. There are plenty at Delta and United too. Nobody is excusing bad service, but if so many of you recognize how miserable and disengaged American’s employees are, how are you not connecting that to leadership?

I don’t necessarily think Isom is a bad guy. He seems to genuinely care about American, and I think he’s done some good things. I just think he’s in over his head. Some people are great at leading teams within an organization but aren’t necessarily equipped to lead the entire organization. I think Isom is one of those people. He’d probably thrive in a different executive role that plays to his strengths, but he’s not CEO material, especially for a brand with the history of American. He doesn’t inspire the workgroup, and I don’t get the sense that he has a particularly compelling vision for the airline.

I’d personally love to see someone like Nat Pieper take over. I’ve been encouraged by what I’ve seen from him so far.

The employees want American to succeed just as much as the shareholders do, if not more. They have entire careers and livelihoods tied to this company. The fact that both pilots and FAs are coming together to publicly demand new leadership should tell you something.

This Overview is Outstanding on finally getting Isom out of AAL immediately! He has failed to listen to Shareholders and AAL Pilots and Flight Attendants. I’ve had executive platinum for around 8 years straight now and I have to say AA has improved greatly during that time, especially this year. No, while baggage services is better, they are still not perfect in my opinion. So whomever is responsible for these noticed improvements does deserve some credit. Is it the CEO, executive leadership, general staff? I don’t know. But they are much better than they have been in the past and that’s what matters most to me and drives me to continue using them as my preferred carrier.

The last group I’d listen to is flight crews. In 2012 they also demanded AA management step aside and allow USair management to run the new airline. They got their wish. One of the best cabin crew I’ve ever seen on any airline was on an AA flight from Doha to Philly (I booked Qatar not realizing that this segment is on AA metal). I wasn’t expecting much but they were such a joy to watch.

#5934. Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

You do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

Generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

Alternatively you can log into your Trusted Traveler Program dashboard, and go to the section that lists your program status. You’ll see the expiration date listed there.

You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

You won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

It costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:

While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

You just have to log into your account on the Trusted Traveler Programs website and update your passport number there. Your Global Entry will then continue to apply with the new passport up until the Global Entry expiration date. See this post for more details on how that works.

On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

To renew your Global Entry membership, you’ll want to go to the Trusted Traveler Programs website, and click “LOG IN” at the top right under the “Returning GE/NEXUS/SENTRI/FAST Member/Applicants” heading.

Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a new Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”

The email as such doesn’t tell you a whole lot, so you have to log into your account again to see the status. There I found out that the application was approved, meaning that there was no need to take part in an interview.

Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

This time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

If you’ve had to renew your Global Entry, what was your experience like?

#5933. American Airlines Pilot Received A Cockpit Alert — An Air Traffic Control Says They’ve “Had Alien Sightings Out There”

A pilot flying from Washington National airport to Philadelphia for American Airlines subsidiary PSA got a cockpit traffic alert near Baltimore. The air traffic controller told him he’d already passed the only airplane she could see nearby. Then she added, “I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…” Listen to Flightdrama’s November 21 recording American Eagle flight 5432 was operaed by PSA on Saturday, November 21, with the Bombardier CRJ-900 (N596NN) taking off from National at 4:27 p.m. and landing in Philadelphia at 4:56 p.m. The controller put the airplane they’d passed at 2,300 feet and said it was flying under visual flight rules. The American Eagle pilot suggested his airplane was “being weird.” And the controller brought up aliens. She said she’d had a couple of reports around Martin State Airport. One pilot had asked what was zigzagging up ahead. On that occasion she remembered getting “no primary target” — nothing reflecting back to her radar from that spot. 0:00 · Pilot “Blue Streak 5432, getting a TA but no tag on it.” 0:04 · Controller “Oh, yeah. No, sir. There is just a VFR that you passed, but he’s at 2,300 feet indicated. There’s nobody around you at all.” 0:10 · Pilot “Gotcha. And the airplane’s being weird.” 0:12 · Controller “I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…” 0:15 · Pilot “Really?” 0:16 · Controller “Yeah. Yeah, pretty much you’re right in the Martin State area. There’s been a couple of them that have, uh, gotten those.” 0:22 · Pilot “That’s, uh, it’s a good story to tell my family. I like that.” 0:25 · Controller “Yeah.” 0:26 · Controller “I had one pilot was like, ‘What is this, uh, what is this, uh, aircraft that’s like zigzagging in front of me?’ And I said, ‘I—there is no primary target. We got nothing on that.’” 0:36 · Pilot “Crazy stuff. Can’t believe that. Could be.” 0:38 · Controller “I know. It’s wild.” 0:40 · Controller “All right, and Blue Streak 5432, so you can switch over to Philly on 133.87. You have a great night.” 0:46 · Pilot “33.87. You too, ma’am. Uh, see ya, Blue Streak 5432.” PSA CRJ-900s taking off at National credit: Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0 When the airliner is at or below 15,500 feet, its system can issue a traffic advisory for another airplane whose transponder replies without giving its altitude. The cockpit display leaves off the data tag. It seems at least as plausible (probably more so) than a UFO. So is a false alert. That said, there were several flase collision warnings approaching Washington National last year, and they were all with an aircraft at exactly 2,300 feet – just like the controller reporting an aircraft at 2,300 feet here. And American Airlines pilots have reported seeing things out the window. Over Arizona in 2018, a Learjet pilot reported something passing overhead. A controller asked American Airlines flight 1095 to keep an eye out. That crew saw something reflecting light several thousand feet above them, too. In 2021, a pilot on American Airlines flight 2292 from Cincinnati to Phoenix described a fast-moving cylinder going right over the top of the jet in New Mexico. American initially told me they couldn’t tie the call to their crew. After a debrief, they confirmed it. The FBI closed its file because it lacked jurisdiction. Listen to American Airlines flight 2292 over New Mexico in 2021 The day before the Baltimore exchange, the Pentagon released 40 more UFO documents and three videos. One 1952 CIA briefing revisits sightings around the airport this flight had just left. That July, Washington National and Andrews both picked up unexplained radar returns. The Air Force sent up interceptors but came back empty. My favorite exhibit from Friday is a single radar slide from a 2023 case. Civilian radar got eight hits in 84 seconds. If one object made all eight, it averaged at least 1,650 miles per hour. Five days before Thanksgiving, the American Eagle pilot already knew what he was going to do with his controller’s report. “It’s a good story to tell my family. I like that.” (HT: Live and Let’s Fly) Topics on this pageAir traffic controlAmerican AirlinesUnidentified flying objectAir forceAmerican Eagle OutfittersArizonaBaltimoreBombardierCincinnatiFederal Bureau of InvestigationNew MexicoPhiladelphiaPhoenixPSA AirlinesRonald Reagan Washington National AirportTraffic collision avoidance system+13 more More From View from the Wing

Listen to Flightdrama’s November 21 recording

American Eagle flight 5432 was operaed by PSA on Saturday, November 21, with the Bombardier CRJ-900 (N596NN) taking off from National at 4:27 p.m. and landing in Philadelphia at 4:56 p.m.

The controller put the airplane they’d passed at 2,300 feet and said it was flying under visual flight rules. The American Eagle pilot suggested his airplane was “being weird.” And the controller brought up aliens. She said she’d had a couple of reports around Martin State Airport. One pilot had asked what was zigzagging up ahead. On that occasion she remembered getting “no primary target” — nothing reflecting back to her radar from that spot.

0:00 · Pilot “Blue Streak 5432, getting a TA but no tag on it.” 0:04 · Controller “Oh, yeah. No, sir. There is just a VFR that you passed, but he’s at 2,300 feet indicated. There’s nobody around you at all.” 0:10 · Pilot “Gotcha. And the airplane’s being weird.” 0:12 · Controller “I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…” 0:15 · Pilot “Really?” 0:16 · Controller “Yeah. Yeah, pretty much you’re right in the Martin State area. There’s been a couple of them that have, uh, gotten those.” 0:22 · Pilot “That’s, uh, it’s a good story to tell my family. I like that.” 0:25 · Controller “Yeah.” 0:26 · Controller “I had one pilot was like, ‘What is this, uh, what is this, uh, aircraft that’s like zigzagging in front of me?’ And I said, ‘I—there is no primary target. We got nothing on that.’” 0:36 · Pilot “Crazy stuff. Can’t believe that. Could be.” 0:38 · Controller “I know. It’s wild.” 0:40 · Controller “All right, and Blue Streak 5432, so you can switch over to Philly on 133.87. You have a great night.” 0:46 · Pilot “33.87. You too, ma’am. Uh, see ya, Blue Streak 5432.”

PSA CRJ-900s taking off at National credit: Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0

When the airliner is at or below 15,500 feet, its system can issue a traffic advisory for another airplane whose transponder replies without giving its altitude. The cockpit display leaves off the data tag. It seems at least as plausible (probably more so) than a UFO. So is a false alert.

That said, there were several flase collision warnings approaching Washington National last year, and they were all with an aircraft at exactly 2,300 feet – just like the controller reporting an aircraft at 2,300 feet here.

And American Airlines pilots have reported seeing things out the window. Over Arizona in 2018, a Learjet pilot reported something passing overhead. A controller asked American Airlines flight 1095 to keep an eye out. That crew saw something reflecting light several thousand feet above them, too.

In 2021, a pilot on American Airlines flight 2292 from Cincinnati to Phoenix described a fast-moving cylinder going right over the top of the jet in New Mexico. American initially told me they couldn’t tie the call to their crew. After a debrief, they confirmed it. The FBI closed its file because it lacked jurisdiction.

Listen to American Airlines flight 2292 over New Mexico in 2021

The day before the Baltimore exchange, the Pentagon released 40 more UFO documents and three videos. One 1952 CIA briefing revisits sightings around the airport this flight had just left. That July, Washington National and Andrews both picked up unexplained radar returns. The Air Force sent up interceptors but came back empty.

My favorite exhibit from Friday is a single radar slide from a 2023 case. Civilian radar got eight hits in 84 seconds. If one object made all eight, it averaged at least 1,650 miles per hour.

Five days before Thanksgiving, the American Eagle pilot already knew what he was going to do with his controller’s report. “It’s a good story to tell my family. I like that.”

#5932. Amex Blue Business Card Bonus: As High As 50K Points Or $500 Cash Back Welcome Offer

At the moment, we’re seeing increased welcome offers on two of Amex’s most lucrative business cards — The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card. Ordinarily these cards have really unremarkable bonuses, but at the moment the offers have been improved very nicely — we’re talking doubled on one card, and more than tripled on the other card. If you don’t yet have either card, this is absolutely the time to apply.

I’ll cover the welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Plus, which I’d argue is one of Amex’s most lucrative and most approachable business cards, especially for those looking to accrue points. I’ll also talk about the Amex Blue Business Cash, which is essentially the cash back version of the card.

Link: Learn more about The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus is currently as high as 50,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of card membership. Apply and find out your welcome offer. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, potentially making this offer worth $850. As a point of comparison, previously the publicly available welcome offer was just 15,000 points after spending $3,000 within the first three months, so this offer is potentially worth more than three times as much. For a no annual fee card (Rates & Fees), this is pretty incredible. This is absolutely the time to apply if you’re interested.

However, as I’ll explain below, the reason you get the card isn’t just because of the welcome offer, but also because of the long term value that it offers. There are lots of great uses of Amex Membership Rewards points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Club, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give some examples of how points could be redeemed:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to generally be among the easiest to get approved for. I also want to emphasize that Amex business cards not counting toward the 5/24 limit really makes the opportunity cost of picking up this card pretty low, for those of us into maximizing our rewards.

The first thing to love about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is that it has no annual fee (Rates & Fees)… you can’t beat that!

But really what makes this card unrivaled within the Amex ecosystem is its return on spending, up to a certain limit. Specifically, the Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1x points. It’s that straightforward. So $50,000 in spending per year would earn you 100,000 Membership Rewards points.

This is the only no annual fee credit card on the market that earns 2x transferable points that can be moved to the full list of airline and hotel partners at the “premium” ratio. There’s literally not another card like that. The one caveat is that the card does have foreign transaction fees, so I wouldn’t recommend using it for purchases abroad (Rates & Fees).

Speaking of the ability to move points to partners, I think that gets at the other thing that’s awesome about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card — in the event that you want to close other Amex cards (with annual fees) that accrue Membership Rewards points, this is a great card to have, so that you can maintain your points balance, given the ability to pool points.

So I view this as a very low risk card to apply for, especially with it not counting toward Chase’s 5/24 limit. The only reason I wouldn’t get this card is if I’m otherwise at the Amex five credit card limit.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Plus Card here.

In the Blue Business portfolio, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is the standout card for me. However, I should also mention the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which is essentially the cash back equivalent:

Personally, I get more excited by the Amex Blue Business Plus Card than the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, simply because I value Amex points at well over one cent each. That’s why I’d rather earn 2x points rather than 2% cash back. Admittedly, not everyone will feel the same, especially those who don’t actually want to put the effort into maximizing points.

The Amex Blue Business Cash bonus is also greatly improved, though, as it was previously for a $250 statement credit. So this is twice as good.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Cash Card here.

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card is a product that often flies under the radar. Ordinarily the card doesn’t have a very exciting bonus, but at the moment, we’re seeing a much better opportunity than usual. The card has a welcome offer as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points. Getting a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1x points) that can be moved directly to airline and hotel partners at the most favorable ratio is something you won’t find on any other card. That’s why this card is in my wallet, and the welcome offer is just the icing on the cake.

Meanwhile if you’re looking for the cash back equivalent, it’s at least worth mentioning the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which has a bonus as high as $500 cash back as a statement credit. That no annual fee card earns 2% cash back (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1% cash back), also with no annual fee.

These are both really lucrative cards that can be worth holding onto in the long run, so if you’re eligible, I’d absolutely recommend applying.

Anyone else love the Amex Blue Business Plus Card, and think it’s an underrated option in the Amex portfolio?

#5931. FedEx Jet Runs Off Miami Runway 80 Days After Amazon Air Crash Killed 5 There

FedEx flight 910 from Memphis ran off the end of runway 26R at Miami airport Wednesday night and stopped in the grass just inside the fence at NW 67th Avenue. From across the street, the nose of the MD-11 lined up with the traffic light. Both people aboard got out safely. Nobody on the ground was hurt. Eighty days earlier, a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Air crossed that same avenue after landing on a different runway. Five people in a van died. Here’s how close the FedEx jet came to the street on Thanksgiving eve, in a photo shared by aviation watchdog JonNYC. FedEx off the runway at Miami https://t.co/WouB3hu13t — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 26, 2026 The plane landed at 8:26 p.m. Eastern. On the tower recording, the FedEx crew calls in to report they’ve gone off the runway. “We see it,” comes the reply. Then the controller turns to another airplane. “American 2199, go around.” Moments later, the controller gives a different American Airlines crew instructions to taxi off the parallel runway. Listen to Miami tower and FedEx 910, and see the flight track. The aircraft was N605FE, named April Star. Here it is at Frankfurt in 2008, via Kambui (CC BY 2.0). Miami had one runway available. The FAA held Miami-bound flights at their departure airports, and its subsequent delay program projected an average wait of 3 hours and 34 minutes for arrivals. At 10:30 p.m. the airport reopened the diagonal runway for departures. The south runway was handling both takeoffs and landings. What A Miami Controller Reported Before FedEx Landed Reporter Anna Giaritelli says a Miami air traffic controller sent her a text before the overrun, while the controller was off duty. They described aircraft headed for Miami and Fort Lauderdale running out of routes around the weather, landlines going down between facilities and more than 10 reports of severe turbulence. “This was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen.” Read the controller’s message and see the regional weather radar. The FAA’s 6 p.m. operations plan shows thunderstorms made Atlantic routes unusable. Miami Center wanted departures routed down the middle of Florida, and controllers had to leave extra space between planes they handed off to Havana because of a communications problem. By 7:43 p.m., the FAA said the Havana equipment problem was resolved. One Boeing 767 crew reported severe turbulence at 8,000 feet about 39 nautical miles south of Miami at 4:24 p.m. At the airport there was light rain, seven miles of visibility and a south wind at 6 knots gusting to 18. Twelve minutes after Fedex landed, the airport reported thunderstorms to the northeast and east. Watch the roadside video of the two aircraft. I determined runway 26R was too short for landing (737 MAX-8). I set up for runway 27 instead (based on surface winds and runway condition code).

#5930. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#5928. Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?

Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

The math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

It's that time of year again: Your last chance to plan your final flights or mattress runs of 2026 in order to snag last-minute elite status for next year.

If you hold Marriott Bonvoy elite status and aren't going to requalify for your status tier this year, there's good news: The program is extending its “soft landing” policy into 2027. With this policy, if you fail to requalify for your current status this year, you will only drop one tier from March 2027 until February 2028.

Related: Marriott elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Based on the program's elite-status policies, the Marriott Bonvoy status you earned in 2025 will expire at the end of February 2027 unless you requalify for your current level or higher in 2026. But what if you don't meet the threshold for the same or higher status?

That's where Marriott's generous soft landing policy comes in. Whether you qualify for a level far below your current status or don't qualify for status at all in 2026, you'll only drop one status tier in 2027.

According to Marriott's website, members who don't requalify for status will see their new, lower tier take effect in early March 2027, and they can enjoy this status through February 2028. Meanwhile, if you requalify for your existing tier or a higher tier, you will also hold this status through February 2028.

This soft landing policy, which Marriott has offered for years, is a win-win: It provides valuable benefits to elite members who weren't able to requalify for status, while giving them a reason to stay loyal to Marriott and perhaps try again for status next year.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Marriott Bonvoy elite status offers some excellent perks, such as room upgrades, late checkout and even lounge access. Thankfully, with this soft landing policy, mid- and upper-tier elite members who don’t requalify this year won’t be left empty-handed. You can still enjoy the benefits of the next-lower tier from March 2027 to February 2028.

For example, with Titanium Elite status, expiring Ambassador Elite members will enjoy many of the same perks of their current status, including complimentary breakfast at most brands, suite upgrades at check-in, 75% bonus points earned on stays and a status match to United MileagePlus Premier Silver status.

You should see your new Marriott status and updated expiration in early March.

#5924. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

We arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

To be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

#5923. TSA Demanded United Airlines Suspend A Pilot Over Terror Support, Union Accused Of Resisting, Report Says

TSA reportedly told United Airlines to suspend a pilot accused of supporting a terrorist group, after the pilots union resisted action according to a federal government source cited by TV news reporter Mike Wagenheim. The new report says the intervention happened last week. The pilot hasn’t been named. Neither has the terror group he allegedly supported. Mike Wagenheim’s November 24 update on the reported TSA intervention Wagenheim’s earlier report cited two sources saying United knew of up to six additional crew members who’d expressed support for terrorist groups. United’s pilots union spokesman declined to discuss individual cases. He said the Air Line Pilots Association has a professional standards committee and legal team that assess accusations against its ethics code and United’s workplace guidelines. The Pilot Israel Barred Was Already On Leave In October, Israel prohibited flights with Sina Amjadian serving as crew from arriving in the country. Israeli officials confirmed the restriction after receiving allegations that he’d expressed support for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah. But United said he wasn’t currently flying, having been on leave since 2024. He flew Boeing 737s and wasn’t qualified on long haul aircraft. Apparently there was material showing Iranian leadership imagery and mourning civilians killed in strikes. There are claims of Hezbollah support and that there was a video of him kissing the regime’s emblem. United Pilot Celebrated October 7 Rapes And Murders As ‘Bravery’ I first wrote about Ibrahim Mossallam in November 2023, after his Facebook description of the October 7 attack as “resistance by a brave people.” United removed him from service with pay but he was reported back flying. On October 6, 2026, after the flydubai pilot sought to use his plane as a missile to attack Israel, United told me: We have withheld this pilot from service pending an ongoing review. There were also reports that he returned after just a day, and that two colleagues had given up first class seats to monitor him in the cockpit. United subsequently denied both accounts. A reported claimed the union blocked his firing. TSA Can Order A Pilot Out Of The Cockpit It was striking that the reported order came from TSA. It has authority that extends well beyond passenger checkpoints. Under federal law, a TSA determination that a pilot poses, or is suspected of posing, a terrorism or passenger safety threat requires the Federal Aviation Administration to take action against the pilot’s certificate. TSA can request that the action take effect immediately. It can also issue mandatory security directives to airlines. However, it isn’t clear from the report what legal mechanism is claimed to have been used and doesn’t report an FAA certificate action. It says the pilot’s “TSA credential” was revoked and describes that as Known Crewmember access. TSA can require an airline to remove someone’s access, but losing that privilege doesn’t mean losing a pilot’s license. Flydubai Shows Why The Concern Is Real I don’t need to know a pilot’s politics. But I wouldn’t want someone who celebrates the killing of civilians at the controls of my flight. That calls their judgment into question even without evidence they’ve planned an attack themselves. The September 30 flydubai cockpit attack makes the concern concrete. The co-pilot of that flight planned a suicide attack on the Tel Aviv airport, attacking the captain with an axe to take over the aircraft. He had satisfied the licensing, good conduct and security requirements for the job, and those checks had failed to uncover his extremist intentions. The values of the person in control of an aircraft matter. @Enough – you really don’t seem to know very much about the topic. Stay off social media.

United Airlines carries cargo consistent with its legal obligations and with U.S. foreign policy. There is no demonstrated connection between that cargo and instances of conflict.

Even the U.N. concluded that the October 7 attacks included rape and gang rape, clear evidence of sexual violence and torture of the hostages. https://apnews.com/article/fe1a35767a63666fe4dc1c97e397177e

Hamas uses civilians as human shields, and hides within the civilian population. They used hospitals as military bases. So while every military conflict includes harm to civilians, frequently at a much greater rate than this one, most of that blame can be assigned to Hamas itself. Whenever you hear about lamentable conditions in Gaza, append “because of Hamas” to the end of that sentence.

Calling Israel’s response to Hamas a genocide strips that term of all meaning. Civilian deaths do not, on their own, establish genocide. The legal question is whether prohibited acts were committed with intent to physically destroy a protected group. Even war crimes do not establish that intent.

Obviously, defeating Hamas and recovering hostages are the obvious alternative explanation for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Israel targets an armed organization, rather than Palestinians because they are Palestinians (indeed, 21% of Israel’s own population is Arab).

And Israel has taken significant measures in its campaign to protect civilians, which is evidence against an extermination policy. They warn civilians in advance of attacks, and evacuate civilian populations. The argument doesn’t even depend on those efforts being ultimately effective to count against a claim of genocide, which is a claim about intent.

There are statements from some terrible people in Israel’s government that are pretty inflammatory (there are some terrible people in our government, or who run for office, who say inflammatory things as well). Those statements do not express operative government policy. Critics often cite National Security Minister Ben Gvir, but most Americans think that’s a military position. It’s not. It’s like head of the police, but he’s been given a more grandiose-sounding title.

The International Court of Justice has held that genocidal intent must be the only reasonable inference from the pattern of conduct. Evidence compatible with other purposes defeats that inference. https://www.icj-cij.org/node/103223

So no, there is not a genocide in Gaza you ignorant fool.
