Scott Kirby is planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and argues fares are still below 2019 in real terms 6; he has said airlines can pass the cost on, helped by Spirit’s collapse removing cheap domestic seats 8. American’s Robert Isom said there is more room to raise fares, and is slowing 2027 growth to protect profitability 6. Ancillaries are moving the same way — JetBlue raised bag fees twice in 2026 4.

Two forces cap the increase. Capacity growth is picking up just as airlines push price, with weak consumer sentiment in the background, Melius Research’s Conor Cunningham warned 8. And the low-cost end can’t follow: Ryanair’s O’Leary said covering his fuel bill would need fares about 20% higher, said he doesn’t expect that, and is cutting costs instead 3.

Europe is on a different clock. Hedges cushioned this year — Ryanair fares actually fell 2% in Q3 — but shorthaul fares inflected upward in August and are now modestly ahead of last year as carriers cut capacity, and the cheap hedges expire in 2027 12.

This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

Structurally higher fuel for three years doesn’t break demand — it breaks the weakest cost structures. Expect fares and fees to stay up, capacity growth to be rationed to routes that clear a higher hurdle, premium and loyalty to carry more of the P&L, and a thinning of unhedged, low-fare operators. United’s Scott Kirby is already planning for elevated fuel through all of 2027 and predicts weaker U.S. carriers will have to cut flying. 12

The pass-through is real but slow. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in the third quarter, up from about 50% in the second and short of the 80%–90% it guided to over the summer, leaving roughly $500 million unrecovered in one quarter 1. Delta attributed its entire 2026 guidance cut — to $5.10–$``{=html}5.60 per share from $6.50–$``{=html}7.50 — to fuel, and about $6 billion in added expense this year 3. Over three years, that lag compounds into permanently repriced tickets: domestic airfares are already up about 30% this year 4.

Three years of expensive fuel is a sorting mechanism, not a demand shock. Carriers with premium cabins, loyalty cash, and hedges reprice and keep flying; unhedged short-haul and low-fare operators cut, shrink fleets, or exit. IAG’s Luis Gallego said strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill — that option isn’t available to everyone.

This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

No single lever covers a fuel bill that doubled in 2026. Fares do most of the work — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, up from about 50% in Q2 — with capacity cuts, bag fees, premium and loyalty revenue, hedging, cargo, and labor cost closing the rest. Carriers with hedges, premium demand, or cargo are coping; those without are cutting flying. 91

Fuel averaged $4.41 a gallon in early November, and was 111% higher year over year in the week ending Oct. 9 311. Revenue at the six largest U.S. airlines rose about 18% in Q3 while operating profit was roughly flat 1.

Raise faresDomestic airfare is up about 30-32% this year. United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3 and expects a similar rate in Q4, having pushed back its 100% target; Q3 fuel rose $1.8 billion, leaving about $500 million unrecovered in one quarter. 3912

Cut capacityAmerican will slow 2027 growth, with Q4 capacity up 5.5-6.5% against roughly 2% at Delta and United. United says it will cut marginal routes; Ryanair cut its winter traffic target by two million passengers and European carriers trimmed capacity, which turned Q4 fares modestly positive. 10112

Ancillary feesJetBlue raised checked bag fees twice in 2026, to $50 from $45 for a first bag booked more than 24 hours out, and a spokesperson said the increase offsets rising fuel and operating costs while keeping base fares competitive. 3

Premium and loyalty mixPremium cabins produced 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion. United’s premium and loyalty revenue each rose 17% in Q3 and contracted business revenue rose 26%. IAG’s Luis Gallego said strong North Atlantic demand lets the group offset its fuel bill. 791

HedgingEurope’s big groups absorbed the spike better because they are hedged — Ryanair at about 80% for the year to March 2027 at roughly $67abarrel.EmiratesstayedprofitableonlyonAED7.1billion($``{=html}1.93 billion) in hedging gains, which cut a 60% pre-hedge fuel increase to 13% net. Hedges expire: Ryanair is only 25% hedged at $95forthefollowingyearandfacesa€2billion($``{=html}2.24bn) fuel increase. 2134

Cut other costs, and sell cargoRyanair is targeting pay freezes, slower pilot recruitment, lower crewing ratios, cheaper airport deals, and more AI in back-office work, after O’Leary said covering the gap on fares alone would need about 20% higher prices. Air Canada recaptured close to 100% of incremental fuel costs through cargo; Emirates’ SkyCargo revenue rose 52% on volumes down 1%. Alaska is cutting 200 back-office jobs. 4513

The lever that decides outcomes is the booking curve, not the tactic. Air Canada’s transborder routes, which book close in, posted a 24% unit revenue surge, while longhaul passengers who booked 60 to 120 days out are flying on pre-spike fares. Recovery lags the price move, so the open question is how much further fares can rise before demand responds — IATA September traffic was down nearly 1% year over year. 5

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

Air India figures submitted to Indian officials; the airline has separately put the cost at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year.

Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian carriers in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack, and the ban has been extended repeatedly 1. Nearly two years on, the economics are visible in three places: fuel burn, network design, and competitive position.

Fuel and block time. Air India told Indian officials the closure pushed fuel costs up by as much as 29% and added up to three hours on some long-haul flights, costing roughly $455 million a year in profit before tax 1. In a separate accounting it put the figure at about INR 40 billion ($423 million) a year 2.

Routes that no longer pay. Air India suspended Delhi–Washington in August 2025 and has struggled to run Mumbai– and Bengaluru–San Francisco efficiently 1. It cut or suspended services to North America, Europe, Australia, and Asia between June and August 2026, citing airspace restrictions and record jet fuel prices 5. IndiGo suspended Copenhagen and trimmed UK flying 6.

Hub geography. The closure has hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, so CEO Tewolde Gebremariam said more Europe and North America flying moves to Mumbai, Delhi grows eastward, and Bengaluru is under study as a third hub 4.

Competitive asymmetry. Foreign carriers that can still overfly Pakistan keep the shorter routings, which makes their nonstop and one-stop services out of India more competitive just as Air India and IndiGo build long-haul networks 1.

The one live mitigation is a northern bypass. India has been negotiating with China for a corridor over Hotan in southern Xinjiang, which Air India estimated could cut its losses by about $1.13 million a week 1.

Separating the airspace cost from the rest is hard. Fuel, the Iran war, and a weaker rupee are hitting at the same time, and IATA put Middle East airspace restrictions alone at 5–20% longer effective flight distances and roughly 2–10% higher operating costs on key Europe-Asia routes as of 2026.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

A Breeze IPO before late 2027 looks unlikely. Neeleman has already pushed his own target twice — from “a window in 2026” to 2027 — and the airline says it doesn’t need the capital, so a listing is about shareholder liquidity, not funding. Fuel is the gating factor: jet fuel doubled in 2026, U.S. carriers are cutting guidance, and airline equities are priced for that. Breeze can wait, and probably will. 325

Breeze is private and does not publish full financial results, so any read here rests on what Neeleman says publicly and on Skift’s reporting around it 1.

Jet fuel prices doubled in 2026, and airline pricing has not found a level that covers the increase — JetBlue President Marty St. George said as much in November 5. United recovered only 72% of its higher fuel costs in the third quarter and now plans for elevated fuel through all of 2027 6. Southwest cut 2026 earnings guidance to $2.60–$2.85 a share from $4, and Delta cut its range entirely on fuel 78.

That matters for Breeze in three ways. Comparable valuations are depressed — Neeleman himself said airline stocks stay cheap because flying is discretionary spend and a leading indicator when confidence falls 3. The sector’s loss cases are loud: Frontier posted a $104 million net loss with an 82% jump in fuel costs, and JetBlue’s bonds traded at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 910. And Breeze’s own cushion is structural rather than hedged — low trip costs, 80% to 90% self-generated traffic, and sole-operator status on nearly 90% of its routes, which gives it pricing room most low-cost carriers lack 111.

Breeze has the profit record an IPO needs and none of the urgency. With fuel suppressing airline multiples into 2027, the rational move is to keep compounding profitable quarters privately and list when the sector re-rates — which argues for late 2027 at the earliest.

What would pull it forward: a sustained drop in jet fuel — the Argus U.S. jet fuel index already fell 13% from $4.90 a gallon on Oct. 22 to $4.27 — combined with a full year of audited profitability and a clean story around the new Priceline-style ground-commerce revenue Neeleman wants to start next year 131.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Breeze’s IPO Timeline, As Told by Its CEO

Breeze posted its first operating profit, in Q4 2024, with revenue up 78% year over year.

Neeleman told Skift an IPO could come as soon as 2026 if equity markets rebounded, but said Breeze doesn’t need the capital — a listing would mostly give existing shareholders liquidity.

At Skift Aviation Forum, Neeleman said Breeze expected profitability the following year and now saw an IPO in 2027 rather than 2026.

Airline Weekly noted Breeze was still chasing annual profitability nearly five years after launch.

At Skift Aviation Forum, Neeleman said Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, and margins ‘in the top tier of the industry.’ He discussed a new Priceline-style revenue model rather than a listing.

The last public date Neeleman put on a Breeze listing was 2027, set at Skift Aviation Forum in December 2025, after he pushed it back from 2026 2. He has not updated that timeline in Skift’s reporting since. At this month’s Skift Aviation Forum he talked about profitability, premium seat mix, AI staffing, and a plan to clip a commission on the economic activity Breeze creates in small markets — not about going public 1.

What has changed is the financial case. Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full results, but Neeleman said it has now strung together four profitable quarters with a fifth expected, and that margins are in the top tier of the industry 1. That is the record a filing would need, and a sharp turn from a year ago, when Airline Weekly was still writing about Breeze’s struggle to reach annual profitability nearly five years after launch 5.

One more consideration: Neeleman is building toward a revenue model that looks less like an airline — taking a cut of real estate and hospitality spending in markets Breeze opens, with first steps expected next year 1. A company mid-pivot on how it makes money has a reason to wait until that line is proven before pricing itself for public investors.

This question was addressed to Luis Gallego, CEO, International Airlines Group.

Not worth it as a package. Finnair is the only strategic fit — and Helsinki’s 50.1% floor means it isn’t for sale. Air Europa is the asset IAG already tried and abandoned after Brussels signaled a block. Norwegian is a Nordic short-haul and package-holiday group IAG has no playbook for. IAG’s own capital discipline argues against all three: Gallego funds projects that beat a 12-15% group margin bar, and these would not. 128

Each target fails on different grounds, and the failures don’t offset each other.

Finnair is the one with real logic. Skift reported a decade ago that IAG was seen as a likely buyer, with Helsinki a counterbalance to London, Madrid, and Dublin 4. That case has weakened. The 2022 closure of Russian airspace severed the Siberian shortcut that made Helsinki-to-Asia profitable, and Finnair is still rebuilding around the wound 1. The Finnish state owns about 55% under a mandate to hold at least 50.1% 1. Finnair also already sits with British Airways and Iberia in a transatlantic joint business, which gives IAG little reason to buy what it already flies with 1. Finnair raised its full-year profit forecast in October on stronger-than-expected demand, so the discount is narrowing anyway 7.

Air Europa is settled history. IAG abandoned the €400 million deal in August 2024 after EU regulators signaled they would likely block it, even after IAG offered to cede more than half of Air Europa’s flights \[\[cite:skn_697884\],\[cite:aw_39375\]\]. IAG would have held close to two-thirds of Madrid seats 6. Nothing in the competitive math has changed, and Turkish Airlines took a minority position in Air Europa last year 1.

Norwegian is the weakest fit. It is in expansion mode, not up for sale — it bought Widerøe and then agreed to acquire Nordic Leisure Travel Group for about $843 million, lifting group revenue nearly 50% to roughly $6.3 billion \[\[cite:skn_828929\],\[cite:skn_824113\]\]. That is a vertically integrated package-holiday business in the TUI and Jet2 mold 3, not the premium long-haul hub model IAG runs.

Finnair’s value to IAG already flows through the transatlantic joint business and a Japan partnership. Extending commercial agreements captures most of the network benefit without a Helsinki negotiation or a Brussels review.

Gallego reviews airline investment proposals twice a year and funds what delivers the strongest shareholder returns against a 12-15% group margin target. Iberia hit a 16.4% operating margin in 2025 on refleeting and A321XLR transatlantic expansion — organic returns IAG controls.

Europe’s distressed assets move on their own terms. Condor’s owner Attestor has openly sought a partner, and airBaltic needed a state loan in April 2026. A smaller, cheaper target clears regulators more easily than a three-way Nordic-Iberian package.

IAG is the most profitable European legacy group and does not need to buy scale it can’t integrate. The one target worth having is the one it can’t buy.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

JetBlue can avoid both a merger and Chapter 11, but the margin for error is thin. It has $2.2 billion in liquidity and about $7 billion in unencumbered assets, enough to fund the JetForward plan through a fuel spike. What it does not have is a buyer — United’s CFO just ruled itself out on JetBlue’s $10 billion debt load — or a second year of negative margins. 12

Survival here is an arithmetic, not a strategy problem. JetBlue has lost money for six straight years and guided 2026 to an adjusted operating margin of negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, cut from negative 2% to negative 5% 2. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $2.8 billion, and it still posted a $257 million net loss 24. The cause is fuel: $4.64 a gallon expected in the fourth quarter against $3.91 in the third, while the $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 24.

The bond market has already priced the risk. Debt maturing by 2031 traded at a record-low 40 cents on the dollar in October, down from about 80 cents earlier that month, and senior creditors hired PJT Partners and Akin Gump Strauss to discuss a restructuring 3. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and what our financial results are demonstrating” 3.

The key uncertainty is fuel, not demand. JetBlue’s premium and cost levers are working — Q3 revenue grew 21%, BlueFirst should add nearly five points of unit revenue, and $30 million of controllable costs came out in the quarter — but none of that closes a gap created by paying $4.64 a gallon. If 2027 fuel lands near the slightly-above-$4 JetBlue assumes rather than $3, the EPS target slips and creditors, not management, set the calendar.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

The conditions that made IndiGo have closed. IndiGo and Air India now hold nearly 90% of domestic capacity, and IndiGo’s own scale — 550+ aircraft and 200 million passengers targeted by 2030 — is the floor Akasa would have to clear. Akasa’s realistic path is a profitable third carrier built on Southeast Asia and secondary routes, not a challenger for the domestic crown. 12

IndiGo’s win came from being the disciplined low-cost operator in a market of first-time flyers, capturing roughly two-thirds of the world’s third-largest domestic market 34. That pool of unserved demand is now largely spoken for. India’s domestic market is more concentrated than at any point in its modern history, with IndiGo and Air India holding close to 90% of capacity 1.

Akasa’s constraints are the ones IndiGo never faced at the same stage: airport capacity limits, restrictive bilateral rights, and a post-pandemic talent shortage 5. Narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until roughly 2033, which caps how fast any new entrant can add metal 6.

Akasa’s one clear advantage right now is network choice. When the Iran war froze Gulf expansion, it redirected to Southeast Asia, adding Mumbai–Hanoi as its seventh international destination and building on Phuket 78. In the first full quarter after the war began, Indian carriers’ international traffic fell about 27% overall, while Akasa grew 26% 9.

The open question is whether Akasa can fund sustained growth through a high-fuel cycle. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, recovering only about 60% of the fuel increase in fares. A subscale carrier absorbing the same shock has less room than the market leader.

The right travel credit card is important for any trip, as it can earn points or miles and provide valuable travel protections. But when you travel for months at a time, other factors — including no foreign transaction fees, international acceptance and benefits you can use outside the U.S. — become especially important.

Living and working on the road without a permanent home base puts these priorities to the test. The best card benefits solve practical problems and remain useful long after a typical vacation would have ended.

With that in mind, these are some of the best cards for long-term travelers and digital nomads.

Now, let's dive into what each of these cards has to offer.

All of the welcome bonus valuations in this guide are based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

The is best for long-term travelers who want broad travel protections, premium lounge access and flexible points in one card.

Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is an excellent card for long-term travelers because it earns at least 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining purchases.

The card's up-to-$300 annual travel credit is straightforward to use, while Chase Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access can provide a place to work, eat and recharge between flights. The card also charges no foreign transaction fees.

Its travel protections are another reason why it's a great choice for digital nomads. Baggage delay coverage, for example, can help cover essentials when your checked bag doesn't arrive on time. Trip delay and trip cancellation/interruption coverage can also soften the financial hit when plans unravel.

Plus, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to hotel and airline partners, including fan favorites like United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt.

However, the card carries a $795 annual fee, and several of its statement credits are tied to particular merchants.

Cardholders can get up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year for qualifying prepaid stays of at least two nights through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, with a maximum of $250 per transaction. It can be a fantastic perk when a long trip calls for a comfortable hotel reset between apartment stays or after a long-haul flight.

If you spend most of the year outside the U.S., weigh the $795 annual fee against the benefits you’ll use regularly.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The is best for digital nomads who can use its extensive lounge network, hotel elite status and premium perks.

Welcome bonus: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards Points after spending $12,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The Amex Platinum comes offers one of the largest airport lounge networks available. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes access to Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required for Priority Pass Select).

That pairs nicely with a high earning rate on flights booked directly with the airline as well as up to a $200 airline fee statement credit every calendar year on your selected qualifying airline (enrollment required; terms apply).

Cardmembers can transfer their Membership Rewards points to Amex's airline and hotel partners, opening up award flights and hotel stays worldwide.

Several other card benefits lend themselves nicely to travelers who stay in hotels, rather than long-term rentals. Hotel elite status, including Hilton Honors Gold Elite, Leaders Club Sterling and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite, can make your stays more comfortable (enrollment required).

The up-to-$600 annual lodging statement credit adds more value to the card and can give you an excuse to add luxe stays to your itinerary. It is split into two up to $300 semiannual credits and applies to qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe, Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®. (Airbnb Luxe and THC require a minimum two-night stay; FHR will also require a minimum two-night stay beginning Jan. 1, 2027; terms apply).

It's worth noting that you likely won't be able to use every statement credit. Someone spending a lot of time outside the U.S. may have trouble using several U.S.-focused perks, including Uber Cash (for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders) and Walmart+.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

The Venture X is best for digital nomads who want premium travel perks and simple rewards on everyday spending.

Welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

For digital nomads, the Venture X works well because of how little strategy it requires, at home or abroad. It earns 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases outside bonus categories. These flat-rate, hassle-free rewards are useful when your spending habits change from one country to the next.

The card allows you to transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel partners. That's even more flexibility when your travels take you all over the world.

The card's $300 annual Capital One travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth $100 toward bookings made through the Capital One Travel portal) are very easy ways to offset the annual fee.

Primary cardholders also receive complimentary access to Capital One Lounges, Capital One Landings and participating Priority Pass lounges.

The card offers cellphone protection when you pay your monthly wireless bill with it (up to $800 per eligible claim, with a $50 deductible and a maximum of two claims per 12-month period). That's useful when your phone is your boarding pass, map and connection to work.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The offers a useful middle ground for digital nomads who want strong everyday rewards without paying a hefty annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months.

At $95 a year, the Strata Premier is the easiest card on this list to justify. Its protections are particularly practical when you live out of a suitcase. The card's 24-month extended warranty can be especially useful when living on the road, as nomadic life can take a toll on electronics and other gear.

Cardholders can transfer ThankYou points to more than 20 airline and hotel partners. There's also an annual $100 hotel benefit per calendar year for a single hotel stay (of $500 or more; excluding taxes and fees) booked through CitiTravel.com or by calling Citi. That's a fast way to offset the card's $95 annual fee.

The Strata Premier offers fewer statement credits than pricier cards. Its $95 annual fee makes it a good fit if you’re traveling on a budget or want an affordable second card.

The is best for everyday spending abroad, thanks to its earning rate on eligible foreign transactions.

For digital nomads, the card's value comes from a benefit that applies well beyond Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights. Cardholders earn 3 Atmos Rewards points per dollar spent on foreign transactions, whether that's a hotel stay, meal, pharmacy visit or souvenir.

You'll also get a 10% rewards bonus on points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

Atmos Rewards points can be redeemed for flights on Oneworld carriers and other airline partners, in addition to Alaska and Hawaiian.

The annual Global Companion Award provides a 25,000-point discount when two travelers book award travel on the same itinerary. Based on our valuations, this benefit alone is worth $400. That's enough to justify the annual fee, even if you never touch the other Alaska or Hawaiian-specific benefits.

Cardholders who spend $60,000 in a card anniversary year can earn an additional Global Companion Award worth up to 100,000 points. Since these awards can be used in any class of service, the larger award could be particularly valuable for a premium-cabin or long-haul partner redemption.

That same $60,000 in spending earns 30,000 status points. Combined with the 10,000 status points awarded after each account anniversary, you'd have enough for Atmos Gold status (mapped to Oneworld Sapphire). On eligible itineraries, that's good for business-class lounge access — even when you're flying economy — priority check-in and boarding, preferred seating and extra baggage.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Summit card.

Many long-term travelers and digital nomads run businesses from the road. These travelers may find it useful to have one or more business cards as well.

One business card that's particularly well-suited to this lifestyle is the (see rates and fees).

This card earns 3 points per dollar spent on travel, shipping, social media and search engine advertising, and cable, internet and phone services (on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The Ink Business Preferred also offers cellphone insurance, primary rental car insurance on business-related rentals and no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

When you live out of a suitcase, the best card benefits aren't always flashy. What matters is what follows you: protections when your laptop dies or your flight gets canceled, solid rewards on everyday spending in any currency and lounges in the airports you actually pass through.

A long list of statement credits might only be great if you'll be back home in a few days. For extended travel, it's more important to pick the card that works wherever you wake up tomorrow.

#5902. Huang’s Surprise Return Doesn’t End Nvidia Questions

President Donald Trump stands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after presenting him with the National Medal of Science in Washington, D.C., October 8, 2026.

Well, that was quick. Less than two weeks after unanimously accepting CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board has now, again unanimously, agreed to reinstate him. This followed “a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.” The first hurdle must have been trickier than the second. Presumably even more importantly, based on “input” from “senior levels” of the U.S. government, the board was “confident” that Huang’s return posed “no national security risk.”

President Trump, no respecter of the division between boardroom and state, was heavily involved in Huang’s reinstallation. In a post on Truth Social, he argued that it was needed “in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

On Monday, Nvidia’s stock jumped by over 30 percent, increasing its market cap by not far short of a trillion dollars. The tech-heavy NASDAQ rose nearly 6.5 percent, the S&P 500 by 4.75 percent. Trump views the stock market as a critical indicator of the nation’s economic health, not without reason, including the “wealth effect” created by rising stock prices. Booms can go bust, but, although calculating the effect of the AI build-out on the economy is not straightforward, by some estimates it may account for a quarter or more of current GDP growth.

Trump also wrote that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Huang’s “return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Trump added that Nvidia “should continue its thorough internal investigation of [its] compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and patriotic duty to protect U.S. national security.” And so it should.

Various government agencies are investigating, as are a number of congressional committees. It was also announced on Monday that the U.S. is prohibiting the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm previously connected to Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese agent with whom Nvidia’s CEO was in a relationship. The concern is that Megaspeed may have been diverting contraband chips to China. More generally, the administration has already tightened the rules governing exports of such chips to other countries where there is a diversion risk, a welcome, if overdue, step, as is the closing of the loophole that allowed enterprises in China and other hostile states to have remote access to the power of advanced American AI chips from businesses located in third countries.

This is a saga with a lot to unpack, much of which remains, at best, guesswork. Nevertheless, we do know (or can be pretty sure that) Nvidia’s board gave Jensen Huang considerable leeway when it came to the way he ran Nvidia, not least with regard to the way that so much of the company’s decision-making was concentrated in him. That may well have underpinned Nvidia’s extraordinary success — a win for the U.S., as well as for Nvidia — but it also clearly played an important part in the current imbroglio and raises troubling questions about the consequences were Huang to step down again or, even if he weathers this crisis, at some later stage. It is said that no man is irreplaceable, but that is not always so.

We also know that Nvidia, sometimes referred to as AI’s central bank, has played a key role in supporting the growth of earlier-stage companies. This has been criticized as a form of circular financing by Nvidia (the company is helping fund some of its client base), but it has played a vital part in the creation of an American AI ecosystem. Through Nvidia, Huang was a critical element in this ecosystem’s growth.

And we know that the success of the American AI sector has geopolitical as well as commercial implications. There is an AI race between China and the U.S. The U.S. must hang on to the lead it has built up — here’s the catch — in no small part with Nvidia’s assistance. Huang has argued against overly broad U.S. restrictions on the export of U.S. chips, arguing that they will only encourage China to make their own, an unconvincing argument given the importance Beijing puts on autarky. Of course, Nvidia would benefit financially (for a while) by selling AI chips to China, but it is not in our strategic interest to allow it.

Huang is entitled to his views, but they do not entitle his company to evade U.S, export controls or even to turn a blind eye should Nvidia’s customers “divert” chips to forbidden destinations. The question of whether this occurred will almost certainly be the main focus of the investigations. It is a question that dwarfs (however much corporate governance purists may object) Huang’s reckless choice of companionship and, in this respect, his lack of candor with Nvidia’s board. The investigations will lead where they will lead. They will also be highly politicized. Regardless of the investigations’ conclusions, they will be a major distraction and, as such, unhelpful to Nvidia and the U.S. AI sector more broadly. That will be a win that should never have been handed to Beijing.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#5901. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#5898. Middle East Tourism Has Split. Which Demand Gets Capital?

Gulf travel now runs at two speeds. Pilgrimage and resort demand held through 2026, while long-haul and corporate travel fell away. Every 2027 capital and capacity plan for the region depends on which market an operator underwrites.

Accor’s Duncan O’Rourke told Skift that UAE city hotels cut rates 15% to 20% in August and September to protect occupancy, while Gulf resort and Holy Cities hotels ran ahead of last year. Then the split moved inside Saudi Arabia. After Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s airport in October, 86% of scheduled departures were canceled and Riyadh RevPAR fell 65% to $65 for the month.

For owners, lenders and investors, the 2027 question is which of those markets to underwrite, and on what recovery date.

Developers kept building. The Middle East hotel pipeline reached a record 771 projects and 188,960 rooms in the third quarter, according to Lodging Econometrics data. Saudi Arabia holds 401 projects, up 15%, and most owners are pushing ahead, though Diriyah canceled a $191 million hotel contract in November. Transactions moved the other way. Knight Frank told Skift that pre-war asking prices no longer match buyer underwriting, and investors are rerunning feasibility studies built on pre-conflict occupancy.

The terms behind that pipeline are changing too. Gulf sovereign funds now expect returns and are phasing projects and selling assets to meet them. Owners are reopening hotel management agreements with operators over performance tests and when management fees get paid. Colliers’ Nicolas Nasra expects the toughest negotiating environment in a decade.

Forecasts disagree by most of a year. Before the October strikes, Accor expected UAE hotels back to pre-war levels by late in the first quarter of 2027. S&P Global Ratings does not expect that before the end of 2027. Since then, Accor has said regional RevPAR may fall about 12% in the fourth quarter, the region’s peak season.

Fourth-quarter results arrive after most 2027 budgets lock in. Every underwriting call made this month carries a recovery date the data cannot yet confirm.

Skift Global Forum East comes to the Grand Hyatt Abu Dhabi on December 9, 2026, with an opening reception on December 8, hosted by Experience Abu Dhabi.

Etihad Group CEO Antonoaldo Neves, Emirates Deputy President and Chief Commercial Officer Adnan Kazim, Rotana CEO Philip Barnes, Minor Hotels’ Amir Golbarg, and leaders from Accor and Radisson will work through these questions with owners and investors placing the same bets.

Complimentary registration is available to approved senior leaders, and standard passes are open to everyone else.

A war has turned the Gulf’s growth story into an open question. Few leaders have settled how trajectory and traveler trust hold under sustained conflict. Skift Global Forum East puts the people making that call in one room in Abu Dhabi.

#5896. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#5892. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#5887. In Praise of Kiwi.com

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Kiwi pioneered a better way to find flights, but the economics of selling and servicing them proved harder.

In September 2019, Skift ran a story with the headline: “Kiwi.com CEO Wants to Build a Rival to Expedia.” Oliver Dlouhý, then 31, was about to speak at Skift Global Forum in New York. The company had just brought in General Atlantic as its majority investor.

Seven years later, Expedia has agreed to buy Kiwi.com for an undisclosed sum. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

What Dlouhý and his co-founder Jozef Képesi built out of Brno, Czechia, was a remarkable entrepreneurial achievement. Kiwi developed some of the most inventive flight search products of the past 15 years.

Founded in 2012 as Skypicker, the company found an opportunity in the fragmented European airline market. Low-cost carriers had built vast networks of inexpensive point-to-point flights, but generally didn't sell connections on one another's planes. Kiwi's technology combined separately tic

Expedia has agreed to buy Kiwi.com for an undisclosed sum, with the deal expected to close in the first half of 2027 subject to customary closing conditions. Founded in Brno, Czechia, in 2012 as Skypicker, Kiwi pioneered virtual interlining — stitching separately ticketed flights from carriers that don't sell connections on one another's planes into single itineraries — along with map-based search and its NOMAD multi-city product. That model carried a servicing cost: when a traveler misses a self-connection, no airline is obliged to rebook them, so Kiwi built its Guarantee, priced the disruption risk, and ran the operations behind it. Skift's September analysis of flight search economics found Skyscanner, which refers travelers to booking partners, was substantially more profitable. Kiwi's revenue fell 20% from €284 million ($331 million) in 2023 to €227 million ($264 million) in 2025, which the company attributed to lower ticket prices; cuts to personnel and customer support spending lifted operating profit to about €15 million ($17.5 million), though it still recorded a net loss of roughly €600,000 ($700,000). After years of disputes — including a U.S. injunction barring it from scraping Southwest's website — Kiwi reached a commercial agreement with Ryanair in January 2024 and said by April 2025 it had more than 200 airline collaborations. Kiwi has said it intends to continue operating as a standalone brand.

#5880. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images)

That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

“It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

Trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

“I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

“You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”

Trump, who was convicted by a New York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

“In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

“This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”

Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”

“The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”

Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

“I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

“I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

“Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”

On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

“You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”

John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

#5875. The House has a new lame-duck challenge: Attendance

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a new challenge: Attendance.

Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

"Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members."

“We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

“I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”

And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

“There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

“I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”

Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

“The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”

A customer shops for eggs at a grocery store on March 12, 2025, in Chicago, Illinois. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

FOOD DELIVERY FAVORITE FORCED TO FORK OVER MILLIONS AFTER DOJ ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST AMERICAN WORKERS

A Kroger grocery store in Covington, Kentucky, on Sunday, June 2, 2024. (Jeffrey Dean/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A young man shopping for groceries at the grocery store. (iStock)

In an October internal memo announcing the 3,000-role reduction, Foran pointed to expanding artificial intelligence and workflow automation as a central driver for trimming corporate overhead.

At the same time, job boards have listed nearly 30 corporate openings for Kroger’s new Global Capability Center in Bangalore across finance, supply chain, real estate and data analytics. Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley previously told investors the overseas capability center would deliver modest savings in 2026 before generating more substantial cost reductions in 2027 and 2028.

#5871. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

Eric Schiffer, CEO of Reputation Management Consultants Inc., believes Democrats are engaging in double-sided messaging by attacking Trump’s efforts to reinstate Jensen Huang.

The Trump administration’s efforts to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia have set a new bar for shaping a private corporation, according to Eric Schiffer, chairman and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, a crisis management and brand protection firm.

"Trump came in to really give a second life to Jensen, where he would have been dead," Schiffer told Fox News Digital Tuesday.

Schiffer said the intervention has opened a kind of Pandora’s box that Democrats may seek to exploit to benefit ideological allies in the private sector. President Donald Trump speaks with Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center Nov. 19, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

#5865. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

#5863. For ‘Denuclearization,’ Trump Should Build Up to Build Down

The president ought to take a page from Reagan’s Cold War playbook.

The U.S. Navy Ohio-class ballistic missile submarine USS Tennessee returns to Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay, Ga., in 2013.

Mass Communication Specialist First Class James Kimber/U.S. Navy/Handout via Reuters

President Trump left his Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin last week still dreaming of a denuclearization agreement with his great-power counterparts. But Trump’s long-held ambition to achieve the deep reductions in nuclear weaponry that Ronald Reagan secured with his Soviet counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s clashes with reality. Chinese and Russian officials may now be speaking the language of “strategic stability,” but Trump would be wise to recognize that these pronouncements are intended to deter him from taking the steps necessary to strengthen America’s nuclear deterrence.

Unlike Gorbachev in the final years of the Cold War, neither Xi nor Putin currently has any appetite for meaningful arms-control negotiations. Xi acts as if his geopolitical position compares favorably with America’s. Both men are wielding their nuclear power to weaken America’s security and dissolve its alliances. Consider Putin’s nuclear threats during the war in Ukraine and Xi’s campaign of coercion in the western Pacific, which is shielded by China’s growing nuclear arsenal.

Kyle Balzer is a resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute where he specializes in nuclear strategy and policy.
